comment: Box 3.1 requires DPI-H components to be "non-transactional… not point-of-care workflow engines or clinical transaction processors." The concern is sound — shared infrastructure should not concentrate control, or make its operator accountable for clinical or financial decisions(§3.6.3) — but the rule is too broad. The draft's own foundational example, payments DPI ("rails for moving money securely and at scale between parties", §1.2.3), is transactional and is bedrock public infrastructure; it meets the concern by keeping settlement and balances with the banks. A coordination or claims fabric (C1, C3) works the same way — it carries the transaction and keeps processing and authoritative decisions with the participants. The draft's own architecture already contains a stateful, lifecycle-tracking DPI-H component: the Public Health Surveillance Platform does "case registration and management… outcome tracking" and contact "follow-up" — so the criterion is not even applied consistently within DPI-H today. We recommend refining the criterion: a DPI-H component may carry transactions provided it keeps processing and control with the participants rather than concentrating them. The other Box 3.1 tests — shared, reusable, publicly governed, open, technology-neutral — continue to hold the boundary.
